lead: IPsec is a set of protocols that protects IP packets at the network layer. It authenticates the sender and can encrypt the payload, so routers and links between two sites cannot read or alter traffic. Each protected flow uses a security association: a one-way agreement holding keys, algorithms and counters. IPsec is common in site-to-site VPNs, remote-access VPNs and host-to-host links. Because it works below TCP and UDP, applications need no change. Some syllabi call it IPSec.
prereq: You need: block ciphers and modes (see Unit 3), MAC and HMAC (see Unit 4), and MITM and replay attacks (see Unit 1).

sections.h3: AH, ESP and the two modes

blocks.text: IPsec has two protecting protocols. Authentication Header (AH) adds a MAC over the IP header and payload. It proves integrity and data origin, but it does not encrypt. Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) can encrypt the payload and can also authenticate it. ESP is the usual choice when confidentiality is needed.

Transport mode keeps the original IP header and protects the upper-layer payload. Host-to-host IPsec often uses transport mode. Tunnel mode puts the whole original packet inside a new packet with a new outer IP header. Gateway-to-gateway VPNs use tunnel mode. In tunnel mode a router sees only the gateway addresses; the inner addresses are hidden.

items: AH: integrity and origin authentication only; no confidentiality.
ESP: confidentiality and/or integrity; usually integrity is also enabled.
Transport: original IP header stays visible; payload is protected.
Tunnel: new outer IP header; original packet is protected.

blocks.text: ESP in tunnel mode has fields in a fixed order: outer IP header, ESP header, encrypted inner packet, ESP trailer and ESP authentication data. The ESP header carries the security parameter index (SPI), a 32-bit value that names the security association, and a sequence number. The receiver uses the SPI to find the right security association.

A security association (SA) is a one-way agreement between two endpoints. One SA protects traffic from A to B; a second SA protects B to A. An SA is identified by three values: the SPI, the destination IP address, and the protocol (AH or ESP). The receiver looks up the SA by SPI and destination address.

Each SA stores the algorithms, keys, lifetime and sequence counter. The sender starts the sequence number at 1 and increments it for every packet sent under that SA. The number is 32-bit. The receiver keeps a sliding anti-replay window, often 64 packets wide. A packet whose sequence number is inside the window and already seen is dropped. A packet older than the window is also dropped. This stops an attacker from replaying a captured packet.

blocks.where: SPI is the 32-bit name from the packet header; destination IP is the receiving endpoint; protocol is AH or ESP.

blocks.text: The Security Policy Database (SPD) decides what to do with a packet. An SPD entry matches selectors such as source IP, destination IP, protocol and port. The action is protect, bypass or discard. If the action is protect, the SPD points to an SA in the Security Association Database (SAD). The SAD holds the live SA parameters.
Common ESP algorithms are AES in CBC or GCM mode for encryption, and HMAC-SHA-256 or AES-GCM for integrity. AH commonly uses HMAC-SHA-256. The exact set is chosen by policy and negotiated by IKE.

Internet Key Exchange (IKE) creates and maintains SAs. It authenticates peers, negotiates algorithms and derives fresh keys. IKEv1 uses two phases. Phase 1 builds an IKE SA for control traffic. Phase 2 builds IPsec SAs for user traffic. Main mode and aggressive mode are phase-1 variants. IKEv2 uses fewer exchanges and supports MOBIKE, an extension for a peer that changes address. Network address translation (NAT) traversal and mobility details are advanced; only a few universities teach them.

The SPD is checked before IKE runs. A packet that needs protection but has no SA triggers IKE. After IKE finishes, the SAD has the SA and packets flow. When the SA lifetime expires, IKE rekeys. This keeps long-lived VPNs secure.

IPsec protects IP packets, not routing protocols. Routing security such as the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is a separate topic; BGPsec is not IPsec. IPsec also does not replace TLS for web applications. TLS works inside the application connection; IPsec works below it. A company can use both.

spec.title: ESP tunnel packet
spec.aria: A tunnel-mode ESP packet has a new outer IP header, ESP header, encrypted inner packet, ESP trailer and authentication data.

examples.question: Host A at 10.1.1.5 sends TCP port 443 traffic to host B at 10.2.2.7. Two gateways use ESP tunnel mode with outer addresses 203.0.113.2 and 198.51.100.9. Which addresses does a router on the Internet see? Which addresses are hidden?
steps: The gateways build an ESP tunnel SA between 203.0.113.2 and 198.51.100.9.
The original packet is 10.1.1.5 → 10.2.2.7 with TCP port 443. It becomes the inner packet.
ESP encrypts the inner packet and adds an ESP header, trailer and authentication data.
A new outer IP header is added: source 203.0.113.2, destination 198.51.100.9.
A router on the Internet reads only the outer header. It sees 203.0.113.2 → 198.51.100.9.
The inner 10.1.1.5 → 10.2.2.7 and port 443 are inside the encrypted payload, so they are hidden.
examples.answer: The router sees 203.0.113.2 → 198.51.100.9; 10.1.1.5 → 10.2.2.7 and TCP port 443 are hidden.

traps: AH authenticates but does not encrypt; ESP can encrypt. A question that asks for confidentiality alone rules out AH.
Transport mode keeps the original IP header; tunnel mode adds a new outer IP header.
An SA is one-way. Two hosts need two SAs for two-way traffic.
The SPI selects the SA; the sequence number stops replay. Do not mix them.
IPsec is not TLS and does not secure BGP. BGPsec and TLS are separate.

quiz.q: What does AH provide, and what does it not provide?
quiz.a: AH gives integrity and data origin authentication for the IP header and payload. It does not encrypt, so it gives no confidentiality.

quiz.q: Why does ESP tunnel mode hide the internal IP addresses from an Internet router?
quiz.a: The original packet becomes the encrypted inner packet, and a new outer IP header carries only the gateway addresses. The router reads the outer header.

quiz.q: An ESP receiver has a replay window from 450 to 513. Sequence number 480 was already received. A new packet arrives with sequence number 480 and a valid MAC. What should the receiver do?
quiz.a: Drop it. The sequence number is inside the window and already seen, so anti-replay rejects it even though the MAC is valid.

quiz.q: Why does IPsec need two SAs for a two-way conversation between two hosts?
quiz.a: An SA is one-way: one SPI, one direction, one sequence counter. Each direction needs its own keys and counters, so two SAs are used.

quiz.q: Which three values identify an IPsec SA?
quiz.a: The SPI, the destination IP address and the protocol, either AH or ESP.

quiz.q: An SPD entry matches source 10.1.1.5, destination 10.2.2.7, TCP port 443 with action protect. A matching packet arrives and an SA already exists. What happens?
quiz.a: The packet is protected by the SA found in the SAD; no new IKE exchange is needed.

quiz.q: What is the difference between the SPD and the SAD?
quiz.a: The SPD is the policy: protect, bypass or discard for matching traffic. The SAD stores the live SAs with keys, SPI, algorithms and counters.

quiz.q: Why must IKE authenticate the peers before ESP sends protected traffic?
quiz.a: ESP keys must be shared only with the real peer. IKE authentication stops a man-in-the-middle from negotiating keys with either side.

beyond: Not for the exam. IPsec appears in cloud VPN gateways, SD-WAN and mobile backhaul. IKEv2 with MOBIKE lets a phone keep a VPN while its IP address changes. NAT traversal wraps ESP in UDP port 4500. Post-quantum IPsec is an active research area.
